paras: The lynching of Noah Anderson took place at New Richmond, Clermont County, Ohio, on the afternoon of August 21, 1895, when a crowd seized Anderson, a Black man, from the village marshal outside the jail and hanged him from a tree. He had been arrested hours earlier, accused of choking to death Franklin Friedman, an elderly bank president. Reports that Anderson was insane drew wide comment, especially in Southern papers.

Friedman, whose name was also printed Fridman and Friedland, was nearly 80, president of the First National Bank of New Richmond and one of the wealthiest men in the county. According to the Associated Press, Anderson had come to New Richmond on a shanty boat a few months before and said he was a paper hanger. The Wichita Daily Eagle reported that he had been adjudged insane in Kansas in 1892 and discharged from the asylum in 1894 as "not in his right mind."

In the Associated Press account, Friedman stopped at one of his houses shortly after noon, walked into a field and was choked to death by Anderson. A second Cincinnati dispatch tied the attack to a quarrel over land beside Anderson's lot, and the New York Sun had Anderson spring from hiding beside the road.

Officers found Anderson at his house and locked him in the small village jail, which a crowd of several hundred soon surrounded, shouting "Hang him!" and "Lynch the coward!" He was reported to have confessed to Marshal Henderson and blamed Friedman for the loss of a fortune, though the Associated Press said the two had no dealings and called this a "hallucination."

About 4 o'clock the marshal and Mayor Dawson brought Anderson out to take him to the county jail at Batavia. On the sidewalk a man threw a rope around his neck, crying "This is no bluff; we must have him," and the crowd dragged him along Washington Street to a tree, where a man described as the leader hoisted the body. This account said Anderson was "evidently dead" before he was strung up; the Associated Press said only that the mob bore him to the nearest tree and "in a brief time he was dead."

The lynchers wore no masks and made no attempt at concealment. The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, which said Anderson "richly deserved death" but at the hands of the law, predicted that "probably no jury could be found to convict them, for public sentiment is with them." A partly lost passage in the Butler Weekly Times called the officers' attempt to move Anderson "in the face of the mob of 300" a "rashness that bordered on participation." No report of an inquest, arrests or indictments appears in the coverage.

White papers ran the Associated Press dispatch on August 22 under headlines such as "Lynched in Daylight" (Seattle Post-Intelligencer) and "Torn from the Sheriff" (St. Paul Daily Globe). The dispatch described Anderson choking his victim "with the power of a demon" and called the lynching "simply an act of frenzy under most aggravating circumstances." A shorter wire, wrongly datelined "New Richmond, Ky.," ran in the New York Sun, and weeklies such as the Ohio Democrat and the Louisville Weekly Courier-Journal reprinted the story for days.

Some headlines took up the insanity reports, as in the Rock Island Argus's "Mobbed a Madman" and the Courier-Journal's "Crazy Negro Hanged." The Alexandria Gazette granted "some justification" for Southern lynchings but asked why "a crazy negro should be lynched in Ohio for killing an old white man." The Daily Texarkanian and the Barbour Democrat taunted Northern papers for passing over this lynching. The Leavenworth Herald listed the killing with lynchings in Kentucky and California to rebut a claim that lynchings had ceased.

The Associated Press placed the murder and lynching on the same afternoon, while the Kentucky-datelined wire put the murder on the previous day and, in the Record-Union, the lynching at 4 a.m. The Western Sentinel, quoting the Greensboro Record, made New Richmond the county seat, named a sycamore and called it "the second lynching of colored men near New Richmond within the past two years," while the Butler Weekly Times named a poplar and called it the third lynching in Ohio's history.

reader.title: Lynching of Noah Anderson
bases: A crowd of several hundred took Noah Anderson from the marshal outside the New Richmond jail and hanged him from a tree after he was accused of murder (A3, A28, A19).

Anderson was killed by a mob that seized him from the marshal and mayor while he was being moved to the county jail (A3, A28); the crowd numbered several hundred (A28, A19) and acted to punish him for the alleged murder of Franklin Friedman (A2, A18).

Three separately worded dispatches (the AP Cincinnati report A3, the 'third lynching' Cincinnati report A28/A19, and the 'New Richmond, Ky.' wire A6) and the Kansas follow-up A24 agree that Anderson was taken from officers at New Richmond and hanged by a mob.

accounts.label: AP Cincinnati dispatch
accounts.gist: Anderson attacked Friedman in a field shortly after noon, confessed, was 'not right in his mind'; a crowd seized him when the marshal tried to move him to Batavia at 4 p.m. and hanged him to the nearest tree; no masks.

accounts.label: Second Cincinnati dispatch ('third lynching in Ohio')
accounts.gist: Friedman stopped near Anderson's lot and the two quarreled over the land; Anderson confessed to Marshal Henderson; a man roped Anderson on the sidewalk and the mob dragged him up Washington Street, so that he was apparently dead before being hoisted.

accounts.label: 'New Richmond, Ky.' wire
accounts.gist: Anderson sprang from concealment beside the road and choked Friedman the previous afternoon or night; the mob lay in wait and took him from officers, hanging him a square away (at 4 a.m. in one version).

accounts.label: Greensboro Record via Western Sentinel
accounts.gist: A colored man choked the old farmer 'Friedland' on his way home and was hanged from a sycamore 'in defiance of every remonstrance'; second such lynching near New Richmond in two years.

accounts.label: Wichita Daily Eagle (Kansas background)
accounts.gist: Anderson had a record of insanity at Newton, Kansas, and believed someone had taken a large sum of money from him.

framing.detail: The AP text ran widely under headlines such as 'Lynched in Daylight', 'Torn from the Sheriff' and 'Justice Was Very Swift', calling the lynching 'an act of frenzy under most aggravating circumstances'.
Rock Island Argus: 'Mobbed a Madman. Lynch Spirit Causes Another Disgrace to Ohio', mocking the excuse of popular 'temporary insanity'.
Wheeling Daily Intelligencer: Anderson 'richly deserved death' but at the hands of the law; no jury would convict the lynchers.

Southern and Democratic papers (Alexandria Gazette, Daily Texarkanian, Barbour Democrat, Randolph Enterprise) used the lynching of a 'crazy negro' in Republican Ohio to rebut Northern criticism of Southern lynching.
Kimball Graphic and Leavenworth Herald cited it as a Northern lynching, the latter against a claim that lynchings had ceased.

record_check.dossier: Two deaths are reported, but only one in the lynching: Noah Anderson. The other is Franklin Friedman, killed in the crime Anderson was accused of; if counted, white_killed should be 1 rather than null.
1 in the alleged precipitating crime (Friedman); none in the lynching itself.

record_check.record: elderly farmer ... hanged him from a sycamore tree ... second lynching of Black men near New Richmond in two years
record_check.dossier: Most reports call Friedman a bank president and one of the county's wealthiest men; only the second-hand Western Sentinel account says 'farmer', 'sycamore' and 'second lynching'. The Butler account says poplar and 'third lynching in the history of Ohio'.
Add dragging (by a rope around the neck through the street). 'Pursuit' is weak: Anderson fled but officers found him at his house; no mob chase is described. No arms are mentioned beyond a rope.
Confirmed: seized from the marshal and mayor on the jail sidewalk during a transfer to Batavia.
Accused of choking Franklin Friedman to death; he was reported to have confessed and was widely reported insane.
Supported by the AP and second Cincinnati accounts; the Ky.-datelined wire and the Daily Texarkanian imply the 20th or early 21st.

info: Wednesday, August 21, 1895, about 4 p.m. (AP and Cincinnati accounts); the 'New Richmond, Ky.' wire places the murder on the 20th and the lynching early on the 21st
New Richmond, on the Ohio River about 20-25 miles above Cincinnati; at the corner of Washington Street and Western Avenue, half a square from the village jail
Noah Anderson, described as 'colored', a recent arrival who said he was a paper hanger; reported insane
Accused of choking to death Franklin Friedman (Fridman), nearly 80, president of the First National Bank of New Richmond; reported to have confessed
An unnamed mob of townspeople; undisguised and known to one another; one man described as the leader
